Volkenroda
FOL-ken-roh-dah
n. (the Thuringian Cistercian abbey of 1131, the first of the order in Thuringia, dissolved 1540)
German Volkenroda, the people's clearing, from Rodung, land cleared of forest.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Volkenroda in Thuringia was founded in 1131 and was the first Cistercian house in that land, a daughter of Kamp on the lower Rhine. Its name records what the white monks actually did: Rodung is forest cleared for the plough, and the abbey was planted in woodland that the brethren felled, drained and sowed. The Cistercian charter bound the choir monks to manual work and not to the collection of rents alone, and for four centuries Volkenroda kept granges, fishponds and a smithy worked by lay brothers. The house was dissolved in 1540 when Thuringia turned to the Reformation; the nave was pulled down, the eastern parts were kept as a parish church, and in 2001 the Christ Pavilion from the Hanover world exposition was re-erected beside the surviving fabric. The dictionary records Volkenroda chiefly for its doctrine of work. Scripture does not treat labour as a penance to be endured for merit but as the ordinary appointment of fallen man, “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19), and the apostolic rule in a Christian community is plain: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). What the Cistercians got right was the dignity of the hands; what they got wrong was the ledger they kept it in. The believer's warrant is “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord” (Col 3:23), and his prayer over the finished field is “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines labour as exertion of body or mind; a grange as a farm with its buildings; assart as forest land cleared for tillage; a smithy as a workshop of a smith; and husbandry as the business of a farmer.

expand to see more

LABOUR, n. Exertion of muscular strength or bodily powers; toil; work done, or to be done.

GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, &c.; a farm-house with the barns and other buildings.

ASSART, n. In old laws, the offense of grubbing up or cutting down forest trees; forest land cleared for tillage.

SMITHY, n. The shop of a smith; a place where smith's work is done.

HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:19 — "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

Col 3:23 — "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;"

Psa 90:17 — "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."

Modern Corruption

Thuringia's first Cistercian house, 1131, a forest clearing turned into granges and fishponds, dissolved 1540.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that labour is an appointment, not a payment. Volkenroda's lay brothers felled timber and dug ponds under a rule that reckoned the work toward merit, and the sentence that undoes the reckoning is “for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19), which makes the plough a creature's duty rather than a creditor's claim.

The live temptation is the opposite error, to despise manual work because it earns nothing before God. Paul will not have it, and commanded a congregation that “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10); the motive he supplies is not merit but the Lord himself, “as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23), and the blessing sought is upon work already done and not upon work offered in trade, “the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew abad (H5647), to labour, to serve; Hebrew maaseh (H4639), a work, a deed; Greek ergazomai (G2038), to work; Greek psuche (G5590), the soul, the whole man.

expand to see more

Hebrew abad (H5647) — to labour, to till, to serve; “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread”, Genesis 3:19.

Hebrew maaseh (H4639) — a work, a deed, the thing made; “establish thou the work of our hands upon us”, Psalm 90:17.

Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, to labour; “if any would not work, neither should he eat”, 2 Thessalonians 3:10.

Greek psuche (G5590) — the soul, the whole inward man; “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord”, Colossians 3:23.

Hebrew kun (H3559) — to establish, to make firm; “the work of our hands establish thou it”, Psalm 90:17.

Usage

"“In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19) — the charter of all honest toil."

"“if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — the apostolic rule in a Christian house."

"“establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17) — the only prayer that fits a finished field."
